@@135881482 <h> Copenhagen completes transition to an entirely electric bus fleet <p> The Danish capital of Copenhagen over the weekend completed its switch to a 100 per cent electric bus fleet . <p> The City of Copenhagen and local public transport agency Movia said the roll out of new electric buses on bus routes 19 and 5C , completed the capital city 's transition to a 100 per cent electric bus fleet . <p> Routes 19 and 5C are the last of 42 bus routes to be switched to fully battery electric following a 2016 decision by Copenhagen City Hall to convert all bus lines to zero emissions . <p> Interestingly , bus line 5C -- the busiest bus line in Denmark and one of the busiest bus routes in the Nordic region , transporting approximately 17 million passengers each year -- had already transitioned to biogas in 2017 , but has now been brought in line with the 41 other bus routes . <p> Image Credit : City of Copenhagen <p> " The fight for cleaner air has been a key issue for me since I entered politics , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 've now completely completed the transition to 100 per cent electric buses , " said Sisse Marie Welling , Lord Mayor of Copenhagen . <p> " It 's a huge milestone that Copenhagen is now a city where public transport is green and neither pollutes nor emits CO2 . It makes a big difference to the climate and the air we breathe every day . " <p> A total of 37 new battery electric buses have been deployed to run on the 5C bus line , according to Movia , with another 15 to be running on line 19 . <p> Movia has also converted the 350S suburban bus route to fully electric , adding 10 new electric buses , bringing the total number of new electric buses brought into operation over the weekend to 62 , enough to reduce CO2 emissions by 2,000 tonnes per year . <p> This also brings Movia 's total number of battery electric buses running across its entire network to 794 , working out to 72 per cent of the company 's total bus fleet . <p> " Congratulations to the Municipality of Copenhage @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> " Of course with the new electric buses on lines 19 and 5C , but equally with all of the municipality 's bus lines now running on electricity . @@135903239 <h> Canberra moves to secure fuel supply as regional shortages bite small business <p> The Albanese Government is introducing new fuel security powers next week to address regional shortages hitting farmers and small businesses . <p> What 's happening : The Albanese Government has announced new fuel security powers , with legislation to be introduced to parliament next week . The measures will allow the Commonwealth to underwrite additional fuel cargoes and strategic reserves to address supply gaps , particularly in regional areas . <p> The Albanese Government is introducing new fuel security powers next week , with amendments to the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Act set to formalise the Commonwealth 's ability to underwrite additional fuel cargoes and other strategic reserves . <p> The announcement , made jointly by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen on 28 March , comes as global fuel price pressures and a doubling in demand have placed parts of Australia 's regional fuel market under significant strain . <p> " While Australia 's fuel supply outlook remains secure over the near term due to the actions @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ been clear : the longer this war goes the worse the impacts will be , " the joint statement read . " We are acting now to prepare and shield Australians from the worst of it . " <p> The government said it is already in discussions with local and international fuel suppliers to help source additional cargoes as needed . <h> Who it is designed to help <p> The government was explicit about who the new powers are aimed at protecting . Farmers , regional communities and the services all Australians rely on are named directly as the priority beneficiaries . <p> The release acknowledged that despite stable national supply overall , global price pressures and surging demand have seen regional fuel markets come under serious pressure , with an unacceptable impact on regional customers who source their fuel through independent and uncontracted supply channels . <p> The new powers are specifically designed to address uncontracted demand , meaning the supply gaps that fall outside existing commercial arrangements and are therefore most likely to affect independent fuel suppliers , regional retailers and smaller operators without the buying power of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be structured to ensure additional supply can be delivered quickly through trusted operators with the capability and networks to reach the areas where fuel is needed most . <p> Export Finance Australia , the government 's deal-making arm , will be empowered to enter contracts of insurance or indemnity , give guarantees , make loans , or enter arrangements needed to help secure fuel supply from international markets . <p> The government was clear about the boundaries of the support . Commonwealth powers will only be used to help acquire additional supply that is valuable for Australia 's fuel security and where it would be cost prohibitive for private suppliers to source on commercial terms without government support . <p> Critically , the support will not replace or subsidise fuel that importers are already contracted to supply . It is designed to fill gaps , not to displace existing commercial arrangements or provide a blanket subsidy to the fuel industry . <h> What it means for your business <p> For small business owners in sectors that depend directly on fuel , the announcement signals that the government has moved from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The practical benefit for regional businesses , farmers and independent operators is the prospect of more consistent supply reaching areas that have experienced shortages , with government backing giving suppliers the confidence to secure additional and discretionary cargoes they might otherwise have been unable to source commercially . <p> For businesses already managing rising fuel costs alongside higher interest rates , insurance premiums and wage pressures , supply stability is at least one variable the government is now directly addressing . <p> The legislation will be introduced to parliament next week . The government said it would continue to pursue every practical measure required to shield the nation from the worst of the current global uncertainty . <p> Small business owners seeking more information on fuel supply conditions and support options can contact the Department of Industry , Science and Resources or visit the Austrade website.

@@135915084 <p> For centuries , the Arctic was considered the exclusive domain of polar bears , exotic marine life and the occasional intrepid explorer . However , as climate change has thawed the polar ice , it has also opened up new shipping lanes and access to the region 's vast natural resources . And US President Donald Trump 's threats to take over Greenland for national security reasons have catapulted the Arctic onto the global stage . <p> As a result , Kenneth Rosen 's latest book , Polar War , could hardly be more timely . Rosen is an investigative journalist whose articles on a range of political and social issues have been published in The New Yorker , The New York Times and The Atlantic . <p> The struggle for control of the Arctic has a long history . With an eye on the longer-term economic gains , in 1867 US secretary of state William Seward convinced a reluctant Congress to approve the purchase of an economically unprofitable Alaska from a deeply indebted Russia . The price was US$7.2 million ( equivalent to about US$160 million today ) @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> The outbreak of World War II highlighted the strategic importance of Greenland , with the United States establishing a large network of bases there , staffed by up to 15,000 personnel . In 1946 , as part of his doctrine of containing the Soviet Union , president Harry Truman even tried to purchase Greenland . Denmark turned him down , but a 1951 defence agreement gave the US freedom to maintain bases there . <p> For all Trump 's bluster , Rosen highlights how ill-prepared Washington is for the race to control the Arctic . Russia is by far the dominant power , with massive military bases on the Kola Peninsula and more than 50 military installations along its Arctic coastline . <p> Murmansk is home to Russia 's northern fleet , which includes an aircraft carrier , heavy missile cruisers , and nuclear and diesel-powered submarines . Russia also has about 50 icebreakers , of which eight are nuclear-powered . <p> In contrast , US military bases in the Arctic are modest and their facilities and hardware are often dated and poorly maintained . The US has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ installations host vessels on a rotational basis . Not all are well-suited for the hazardous Arctic conditions . And in Greenland , the US has only the Pituffik Space Base , an observation post with fewer than 200 personnel . <p> The US is currently operating just two heavy icebreakers and lacks an established capacity to build more . Consequently , it rushed last year to order new ones from Finland . In contrast , Canada has 18 icebreakers , and even China has four large icebreakers in service with at least two more nearing completion . <p> Despite being far from the region , China assertively claims to be a ' near-Arctic nation ' and has observer status in the eight-member Arctic Council . In 2018 , China approved an Arctic policy which includes a plan to open a Polar Silk Road . <p> Rosen 's field work was thorough , taking him to Alaska , Canada , Finland , Greenland , Iceland , Sweden and the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard . He also spent time on two US Coast Guard vessels and a Norwegian icebreaker , taking careful @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Comparing Russian and US capabilities , the captain of the Norwegian icebreaker confirmed to Rosen that Russia is ' the boss in the Arctic . ' The US Coast Guard captain described the US as ' an Arctic nation that does n't know how to be an Arctic nation . ' <p> Russia 's war on Ukraine was a wake-up call for the far north . In response , Finland joined NATO in 2023 , and Sweden followed in 2024 . Both have stepped up their military presence in the region . Finland has maintained compulsory military conscription for more than a century and has a large and well-equipped reserve , whereas Sweden abandoned conscription in 2010 and has a lot of catching up to do . <p> Rosen reminds us that the race for the Arctic is about much more than national security . Russia currently dominates the Arctic Sea route which , if fully opened , would allow ships to circumvent the Suez Canal , shortening maritime travel between East Asia and Europe by around two weeks . The region also has large untapped oil , gas and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ if these resources are poorly managed , they could cause untold environmental damage . <p> Part travelogue and part strategic analysis , Polar War would have benefitted from a few maps and tables setting out the strategic assets of the major political players . Rosen 's prose is occasionally chatty , but this in no way detracts from the importance of his message . <p> The US has neglected the Arctic for too long and needs to catch up in a hurry . To do so , it would be well advised to work closely with its Arctic allies , who have far more experience and are better prepared . Polar War is essential reading for anyone wishing to understand this rapidly emerging geopolitical hotspot . <p> Author <p> Robert Wihtol is an adjunct faculty member at the Asian Institute of Management and former Asian Development Bank country director for China and director general for East Asia . <p> Image of a Royal Danish Navy frigate , HDMS Triton , passing an iceberg in the waters around Greenland : NATO/Flickr.

According to senior Liberals , the slideshow is proof Taylor is still more a management consultant than a politician . <p> The graphs are supposed to represent Taylor 's preparation for his first budget reply speech , although to colleagues they represent confusion and a man without a capacity to communicate a clear political narrative . <p> " What he 's very good at is pulling apart businesses and rebuilding them , and I worry that he 's leaning too hard into that and basically overcomplicating things ... He has little instinct for what lights up voters and how to get their attention . " <p> With opinion polls showing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on Taylor to find a coherent political message is becoming more pressing . If the party is to have any hope , he needs to re-establish the economic credentials lost during the previous parliament . <p> The latest Australian Financial Review/RedBridge Group/Accent Research poll shows the Coalition 's primary vote has fallen to a record low of 17 per cent , down two percentage points since February , when Taylor toppled Sussan Ley to become Liberal leader . One Nation has climbed to 29 per cent , just three points behind Labor 's 32 per cent primary vote . <p> On Taylor 's left flank , Liberal moderates are grumbling that he is not making use of his shadow treasurer , Tim Wilson . The Victorian MP 's lack of presence in Question Time over the past four parliamentary sitting weeks has not gone unnoticed . <p> " We have n't bothered to have a question from the shadow treasurer in the last Question Time before the budget , " Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told parliament on Wednesday . " It shows that their focus is not on talking Australia @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's colleagues expressed concern this week that Taylor 's experience in economic portfolios -- he was shadow treasurer for three years under Peter Dutton in the last term -- has made him reluctant to let go . <p> " Tim knows how to talk to people , " one Liberal moderate tells The Saturday Paper . <p> " He gets retail politics in a way that few people on our side understand . Taylor does n't seem to consult him much either . He gets retail politics in a way that few people on our side understand . The problem is he is being kept in the background ... Taylor does n't seem to consult him much either . " <p> Topping the list of things that Labor wo n't let Wilson forget is a withering attack on the tax system he delivered to parliament in 2018 , which the government is using to buttress its own arguments for tax reform policy proposals being floated ahead of the budget . <p> " Today it 's time to be honest : the tax system is screwing over young Australians . " In short : if you work hard to get ahead , you get hit hard ; if you live off assets , you do n't . " <p> With Albanese and Chalmers both flagging possible changes to the capital gains tax discount in the budget , a move aimed at giving younger Australians a better chance of getting into the housing market , Wilson 's 2018 words will make it harder for the new shadow treasurer to oppose a budget measure designed to address that same imbalance . <p> Chalmers has also made hay with Wilson 's record on other issues , such as superannuation . <p> In a 2019 appearance on The Bolt Report , Wilson suggested that compulsory superannuation may not be serving the interests of low- and middle-income earners , arguing some workers might be better off taking the money as income in order to make it easier to pay down debt such as a mortgage . <p> " We 're pouring more and more money into superannuation each year . Analysis by the Grattan Institute , of all people , has highlighted that most @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Wilson told Andrew Bolt . " Some of us are saying for low-income earners or even for medium-income earners in particular it might make more sense that they have at least the choice to be able to take that money instead of taking it as more super -- putting it towards their wages just to be able to do things like pay down debt , particularly on a house . " <p> Whether or not Wilson 's argument has merit , it blunts his ability to argue against Labor 's recent changes to the way superannuation is taxed , which introduced a higher concessional rate of tax for about 90,000 people with the biggest superannuation balances . <p> Then there is Medicare , Labor 's policy talisman , which has been a central pillar of its election strategy for decades . <p> In 2011 , five years before he entered parliament , Wilson wrote a piece for online news and opinion website The Punch , arguing that instead of continuing to provide universal health financing the government should " restructure our health system toward a bottom-up individual health account system @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an individual health account that they contribute to on a periodic basis from their income , like superannuation . " <p> Despite the fact Wilson has never repeated the proposal , it has n't stopped Chalmers and other Labor ministers from arguing that Wilson 's real agenda is to privatise Medicare . <p> Wilson 's supporters reject the suggestion he is being sidelined . Those close to him argue that the fuel crisis has simply consumed the political oxygen and asking questions in parliament about the budget or the government 's handling of the economy would have been a waste of good ammunition . <p> Wilson 's view , which he has shared with those close to him , is that the intensity of Labor 's focus on him is a confirmation of his effectiveness . <p> One anecdote Wilson regards as a compliment , and which he has repeated to colleagues , is of a recent conversation with a Labor MP who told him : " We 'll do Taylor slowly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be unstoppable . " Right now , I want to see more crude oil ... more gas ... more houses . And that has to be an imperative for this budget . @@135973525 <h> The difficult path to a gas tax <p> While Liverpool Plains farmer Sally Hunter was saddling up her horse Broccoli on March 16 for a community protest , liquefied natural gas traders in the Asian market were waking up to a 20 per cent leap in the price of futures contracts . <p> By the time Sally and Brocky rode into the Lower Hunter Valley last weekend , they had covered 400 kilometres along the proposed route of a Santos pipeline stretching from Narrabri to Newcastle , speaking with dozens of landowners along the way . <p> Hunter says landowners are opposed to hosting the pipeline , " locking us into this infrastructure that gas users will be paying off for 30 years " . <p> In the meantime , an Iranian missile strike had knocked out the Ras Laffan LNG facility in Qatar . The nature , duration and scale of the Iran war 's impacts are still unclear , however , according to Josh Runciman , lead gas analyst at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis . <p> " Electricity markets are already pricing in rising fuel costs , and we 've seen that in the futures market . So we 're in this really uncertain situation -- we do n't quite know what 's going to happen to domestic gas prices , " says Runciman . <p> The Albanese government is currently consulting on the design of a gas reservation scheme , which will require LNG exporters to keep a portion of their product as conventional gas for the domestic market instead of selling it overseas . @@135973535 <h> John Hewson How to deal with the oil price shock <p> Another world oil crisis , another period of stagflation -- the combination of sluggish economic growth and rising unemployment with accelerating inflation . The current crisis , the direct result of the divisive and controversial war waged by the United States and Israel against Iran , is likely to be the worst yet . The biggest upheavals prior to this arose from the Yom Kippur War in 1973 , when major Arab oil nations cut production and refused to sell to countries supporting Israel , and following the 1979 Iranian Revolution . Oil prices almost quadrupled , inflation reached 18 per cent and unemployment 10 per cent , and the 1980s brought deep recession . <p> At the time of this first shock , I was wrapping up my tenure as an economist at the International Monetary Fund in Washington , DC . I remember I had a Buick V8 at the time , a gas guzzler , and I found myself queuing for hours just to get about a half tank injection . I returned to Australia @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- which I opted for rather than accept a position with the Treasury or go into academia -- certainly a sliding doors moment for me . <p> One of my final tasks at the IMF was to assist in what were the early stages of global economic forecasting . We were working through the official forecasts of major economies in an attempt to bring them together to form a world view . This was a very challenging time at the IMF , with the oil shock coming on top of the collapse of the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates . On my arrival at the RBA , then deputy governor Harold Knight asked me to do a private review of the central bank 's recent forecasts . <p> My overall impression was that they had n't understood the magnitude or significance of the global structural shifts that were occurring . While I ca n't recall the actual numbers , they suggested a fairly modest " blip " down in economic growth and a modest " blip " up in inflation and unemployment , with the impression that they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ was we were entering a period of stagflation that would be a continuing challenge to both fiscal and monetary policies , probably for many years to come . <p> More broadly , I was struck by just how uncompetitive and inward-looking we had become as an economy , seemingly hoping to step around the global internationalisation of domestic financial systems , with deregulation and depoliticisation of financial markets , market-determined interest rates and more exchange rate flexibility . <p> There were a number of exchange rate crises in Australia in the 1970s , when governments and the authorities sought to defend our peg to the US dollar and , when that proved impossible , to then devalue the Australian dollar . I became intent on calling , both from the Reserve Bank and subsequently as an adviser to treasurers Phillip Lynch and John Howard , for a complete reform of our financial system and financial policy processes . This finally led to the establishment of the Campbell Committee under the Fraser government . <p> If such times are ripe for reform , Australia is overdue in terms of its energy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ already described by International Energy Agency chief Fatih Birol as the worst in history , has forced many importers around the world to take various measures to ensure supply and cushion consumers and business from the price effects . Goldman Sachs is among Wall Street banks forecasting that the persistence of supply disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz through April will push oil prices above US$150 a barrel . The Reserve Bank said this week inflation in Australia will reach 5 per cent by midyear . <p> Not surprisingly , the RBA was caught somewhat short and must now consider the damaging impact on the economy of fuel and fertiliser shortages . The March increase in interest rates , made mostly in the context of the unexpected rekindling of domestic inflation , has come as a " double whammy " , as Mike Seccombe described in these pages , citing The Australia Institute 's Matt Grudnoff -- compounding the oil price shock and damage to our growth capacity . In the 1980s it was aggressive hikes by then Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker that finally got inflation under control -- only after it reached as high as 20 per cent . We are in a stronger inflation-targeting environment today . It 's important to note , though , that the far more potent force pushing inflation lower through the ' 80s and ' 90s -- though Donald Trump would hate to admit it -- was China flooding the world with cheap manufactured products . This is no longer the case today . <p> Recession is not a solution to inflation , and the RBA risks going too hard too fast if it does what economists are beginning to project and raises interest rates two more times . <p> Surely the overriding imperative of an effective response to oil shocks is a longer-term strategic plan that not only deals with the more immediate impacts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ security . By Matthew Griffin . <h> Suburban hero : multidisciplinary artist Jon Campbell <p> People used to paint their own signs . I do n't mean just shop names but everything from gig posters to banners they planned to hold up at sporting events . These amateur sign painters would have to work out how to fit a bunch of letters into a defined space . They would have to make all sorts of aesthetic decisions -- colour , scale , font and so on -- and then display the results in public . <p> There is a shift in the way you write once words get to a certain scale . Handwriting does not work on a sign . You ca n't support your hand 's weight with the side of your palm . You need to move your whole arm like a teacher at a blackboard . People do n't really use their hands like that anymore . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ up family photos . These days , it seems as though everyone has a computer and a cousin who knows how to use it . You get to choose between Arial and Times New Roman , but that 's it : the rest of the decisions are made for you . Then you print it , the lines are straight and the letters are centred . It looks " professional " , whatever that means . It 's now possible to walk down a shopping strip and see no trace of a hand at all . <p> Before AI , before mobile phones , before the internet , Jon Campbell was painting . I do n't mean signs , I mean " Painting " painting . When I met him , 20-something years ago , a mutual friend introduced him like this : " This is Jon , he 's a great Painter . " For the record , Jon Campbell is one of my best friends . I will not pretend to be impartial . <p> Although Campbell is primarily a painter , he works across a range of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ neon , textiles , printmaking , the list goes on . His subject matter varies but a few recurring themes have emerged throughout his career . His upbringing in Melbourne 's western suburbs is a continuing source of inspiration . Campbell 's artworks often use text . Words are abstracted to the verge of illegibility in both the shape of the individual letters and also through the manipulation of the words themselves , through contraction and exaggerated phonetic spelling . They 're full of local parlance and slang , the poetry of the suburbs . The word " kebabs " is treated with the same reverence as " Sam Kerr 's Left Calf " . <p> Campbell currently has a survey exhibition titled yEAH ? / ? dU N NO at Geelong Gallery . It sums up his infectious enthusiasm . <p> At a time when everybody seems to have an opinion about everything , " Du n no " is refreshing in its uncertainty . It 's disarmingly honest . @@135973537 <h> Tom Holloway 's Beyond the Neck remains bleakly relevant <p> Thirty years ago , Martin Bryant took two semiautomatic rifles to the Port Arthur Historic Site and shot 58 people , killing 35 . In response , the newly elected Liberal government of John Howard overhauled Australia 's gun laws , heavily restricting automatic and semiautomatic weapons and establishing a gun registry and a waiting period for purchase . <p> Playwright Tom Holloway was 17 years old and living in Tasmania at the time . His play dealing with the horror and grief of the mass shooting was originally supported by La Mama in 2004 and premiered in Hobart at the Peacock Theatre in 2007 . It 's based on in-depth interviews with survivors and Holloway 's recollection of the massacre 's impact on the country . <p> Set 10 years after the shocking event , it shows us four characters returning to the scene to confront their individual traumas . It won the AWGIE for Best Stage Play in 2008 and would be rightly described as a modern classic of the Australian theatre canon . <p> Now , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Neck is being remounted at Theatre Works in St Kilda to mark the 30th anniversary of the tragic killings . Director Suzanne Chaundy , a titan of independent theatre in Melbourne , and Theatre Works executive director Dianne Toulson both argue it is a work that demands to be remounted . ( Chaundy is in a position to know the play well , since she directed a remount of it at Red Stitch in 2012 . ) <p> With the shootings at Bondi last December still echoing throughout the culture , it 's depressingly easy to see why . Holloway is a master of the depressing play . Beyond the Neck fits easily alongside Red Sky Morning -- also programmed at Theatre Works this year -- Love Me Tender , Fatherland , And No More Shall We Part and Do n't Say the Words , each of which has over the years filled me with a terrible sense of hopeless dread . <p> The stage is set simply , with four wooden chairs on a floor painted to look like slabs of white marble . Behind is a large painting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ distance among the green trees and hills and across the crystal blue waters of Mason Cove , the natural beauty of the landscape contrasts murkily with the site 's brutal history . Taken altogether , it suggests a museum or a gallery . <p> The mid to late 2000s in Australian playwrighting generally adopted a post-dramatic aesthetic influenced by British In-Yer-Face writers such as Sarah Kane , Mark Ravenhill and Martin Crimp . That influence is very strong in Beyond the Neck , employing direct address and declarative statements throughout . This creates a structure of ironic distancing that supports a deliberate avoidance of drama , replaced instead by pained and prolonged introspection . <p> It is important not to look away from our past but instead to imagine it in all its complexity and contradiction to try to make sense of how we got here and who we have become . <p> It follows four characters : a tour guide ( Francis Greenslade ) who witnessed the shootings , a mother ( Emmaline Carroll Southwell ) who lost her family in an unrelated car accident , a young boy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ him do terrible things , and a teenage girl ( Cassidy Dunn ) who lost her father in the shooting and has fallen prey to conspiracy theories and argues that the shooting was a false flag conducted by the government . <p> Though the older characters have an authority to their grief born of actual or imagined proximity to disaster , it is the two younger characters who turn out to have real depth in this contemporary production . The young boy struggles with violent ideation and chronic dissociative traits , which in 2006 were still considered isolated cases of concern . In the intervening years that confused rage has metastasised globally by feeding into the manosphere online and creating a terrifying movement of weaponised misogyny . <p> Likewise , the conspiracy theorising that obsesses the teen girl has shifted from a fringe belief into mainstream social practice . Weaving complex symbolic connections around our trauma has become all too common a prophylactic against processing our personal and societal damage . <p> The shooting took place on a site of historic cruelty and bloodshed in the name of imperial progress @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the iconography of colonial power , of our colonial past . This adds an extra layer of ironic distance that dissects and displays human pain but offers neither panacea nor prognosis . <p> Performances are uniformly strong , though there is little detail for them to work with : the depth of character is found in the repetitions , corrections , interruptions and awkward silences that have always been a hallmark of Holloway 's work . The actors talk over each other and claim the stage from each other as the individual stories blur and become a grim meditation . <p> As a metaphor for white violence , how it repeats and how we studiously avoid talking about it , Beyond the Neck remains powerfully relevant today . There are light moments with gently comic turns of phrase scattered throughout , but I find they serve less as a respite from and more as a fleeting contrast with the dark atmosphere of the play . <p> Richard Vabre 's lighting design with Philip Mcleod 's composition and Jack Burmeister 's sound design fill the empty dark spaces of Emma Ashton @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the prison , the museum and the mausoleum . Everything is unsettling . <p> Chaundy 's direction leans into this and draws out the rhetorical movement of the dialogue that the work emphasises in place of any narrative progression . Though the work is ostensibly set in 2006 , it is a reflective moment , and the characters are each in their way trapped in it . The tragedy is frozen in time and place by a kind of national memorialising to which , of course , Beyond the Neck contributes . There is a rhetorical distance always between the text and the history that is clouded by the obscured relationships between the characters . It creates a feeling of chaos and horror that remains chilling nearly 20 years later . <p> I would n't describe it as a fun show to watch , obviously . If you 're looking to escape the darkness choking our world for a few hours , Beyond the Neck is probably not going to be your first choice . Nevertheless , it is important not to look away from our past but instead to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to make sense of how we got here and who we have become . Holloway 's work has always been at its best when this is his material . Seeing it again after all this time , I 'm mostly left with an impression of how much and how little the world has changed . <p> Beyond the Neck , at Theatre Works , Melbourne , closes today , April 4 . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on April 4 , 2026 as " Post-mortem " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@136049113 <p> In a high-end fashion store or luxury car showroom , the term " vegan leather " sends a strong message of quality . For many shoppers , it promises the look and feel of real leather without using animal skins . As brands move away from animal leather , " vegan " has come to suggest something that is both kinder to animals and better for the planet . <p> However , the reality is more complicated . While these materials remove animal products , they often replace one environmental problem with another . Vegan leather is not one material , but a broad label that covers everything from plastic coatings to plant-based surfaces , which is why regulators are starting to question vague green claims . <p> The appeal of leather alternatives is easy to understand . Concerns about animal welfare , climate change and deforestation have pushed shoppers and brands towards options that seem more responsible . <p> As a result , " vegan leather " is often seen as the better choice -- even though how long it lasts , and where it ends up , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> For decades , these materials were known as " pleather " or vinyl . Today , better finishes have turned thin plastic films into convincing leather lookalikes . <p> When the surface of a PU-coated bag cracks or peels , the damage is more than cosmetic . As the coating breaks down , it sheds microplastics into the environment . <h> The plastic underneath the plants <p> In response to concerns about plastic , new fake leather materials have been developed from pineapples , mushrooms , apples , grapes and even cacti . These bio-based options are often sold as the sustainable answer . <p> Ever wondered what " organic " , " conscious " and " circular " labels really mean ? We asked three fashion experts for guidance on shopping with a clear conscience . <p> However , using a plant does not automatically make a product better for the environment . <p> The issue lies in how these materials are made . A " pineapple leather " shoe may be praised for its plant fibres , but those fibres are usually held together with plastic resins @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a mixed material that can not be recycled in Australia , even though marketing often focuses on the plant ingredient and hides the plastic underneath . <p> Even then , many of these materials break down sooner than real leather and can not be properly repaired . Traditional leather can be conditioned , patched and allowed to age over time , but plant-based alternatives tend to fail once the surface coating cracks or peels . <p> A mushroom- or apple-based bag also can not be composted because of the plastic beneath its surface , meaning it reaches disposal much sooner . Some plant-based vegan leather products have reported life spans of as little as two years . <p> This points to a broader issue . In a circular economy that prioritises reuse , repair and material recovery , sustainability is about keeping products in use and at their highest value for as long as possible . <h> Brands must walk the talk <p> The problems hidden by elusive marketing labels are becoming harder to ignore . The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission ( ACCC ) has made it clear broad @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ must be backed up with evidence . <p> If brands use the word " vegan " to suggest lower environmental impact , they must be able to prove that claim by looking at the product 's full life cycle . <p> At the same time , the Productivity Commission 's 2026 inquiry into the circular economy highlights Australia 's growing problem with products that can not be recycled . As product stewardship schemes expand , durability , recyclability and what happens to a product at the end of its life will matter as much as animal welfare . <h> The ethical distinction <p> None of this means animal leather comes without environmental or chemical costs . These include methane emissions from livestock and the toxic chemicals used in tanning . For many consumers , avoiding animal-derived materials is still an important ethical choice . <p> However , " vegan " and " sustainable " are not the same thing . One describes what has been left out of a product , while the other describes how that product performs over its entire life . Treating the two as interchangeable can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is a call for material honesty . Sustainability ca n't be reduced to a single word or ingredient . It 's measured by how long a product stays useful before it needs to be thrown away . A bag that avoids animal materials but breaks down within a few years simply creates waste sooner . <p> If vegan alternatives are going to be sustainable , they must be designed to last . Sustainability is measured in years of use , not words on a tag . <p> Caroline Swee Lin Tan is an associate professor in fashion entrepreneurship at RMIT University and Saniyat Islam is an associate professor in fashion and textiles at RMIT University.This piece first appeared on The Conversation .

@@136050309 <p> Rising geopolitical uncertainty and complexity demand new approaches to strategic planning , risk management and scenario planning . Traditional methods are becoming less useful for government agencies , organisations and businesses as trends become less reliable indicators of disruptive changes . It 's no longer enough to rely on forward projection of trends as this does n't anticipate shocks , which are increasingly common . <p> Instead , forecasters should consider wildcard scenarios : high impact , low-probability events , also called ' black swan ' or ' long tail ' events . By analysing more extreme scenarios , organisations can better prepare for dramatic changes and become more resilient . <p> Traditional forecasting approaches to scenario generation are based on inductive reasoning , which starts with specific observations and draws a general conclusion . They involve examining political , economic , social , technological , legal and environmental trends ; considering major uncertainties ; and generating the ubiquitous two-by-two matrix of near-term possible worlds . Forecasters then examine how the decision or strategy reflects across these scenarios . Governments , academics and analysts in large corporations still use @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ long-term trends ( 10 to 20 years out ) . <p> Stable , long-term trends -- such as those seen in population changes , climate change or deep technology research -- are not subject to change on a whim and can be anticipated through rigorous analysis . Examples of conclusions from such trends include : 25 percent of global population will be African by 2050 ; the population of developed countries will have gone into a steep decline ; and the effects of climate change will be even more irreversible . However , these techniques offer limited value for shorter-term organisational planning . <p> We are entering a new phase of global order , marked by fragmentation and rapid technological disruption . The United States , the global hegemon since the end of the Cold War , is increasingly being challenged . The international rules-based order is becoming more fragmented and marginalised . China is asserting its regional and global dominance , for example by standing up to US tariffs . At the same time , technological adoption and experimentation ( as we have seen with AI ) can now @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , the analysis of these global trends only sets the stage for more complicated and shorter-term decisions . This is where it gets hard . <p> Instead , decision makers and leaders should use wildcard scenarios to test and improve organisational resilience . Wildcard events break established patterns and therefore do n't rely on historical trends . Using truly out-there scenarios will better prepare organisations for major shocks . The goal is agility and recovery , rather than preparing for any specific event as the underpinning causes will be unique , hard to predict and likely unavoidable . <p> Planners should consider these plausible disruptive and technology-driven shocks that could take place within the next few years : solar flares wiping out satellite communications and telecommunications infrastructure ; fusion power providing near limitless clean energy ; quantum computers breaking traditional encryption ; a large-scale synthetic biology accident occurring ; and a runaway space-debris cascade leading to the loss of all satellite-based services . <p> Some will argue that wildcard scenarios are not truly wild , as trends always come with early warnings and indicators . As science fiction author William @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- it 's just not evenly distributed . ' This is , of course , true . But this argument misses the point of forecasting and futures analysis more generally . <p> The goal of forecasting is not to be accurate or even predictive . Rather , it is one tool to help decision-makers robustly test and thoroughly examine the different decisions across a variety of possible scenarios . There are many other analytical tools and techniques that can achieve the same outcome . It is easy to look back and say what should have been done . The hard part is having the conviction to do it in the first place . <p> Despite the scenario planning that undoubtedly predicted the possibility of new land-based conflict in Europe before 2022 , various strategic reviews did not sufficiently resource the response to the Russian invasion of the Ukraine . It is n't the scenario 's fault if decision-makers do n't act on the findings . This is why scenario exercises should always be tailored to the decision or organisational challenge you face . <p> Rather than just looking at the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ you would regret not doing to mitigate a scenario in the first place . If a business decision makes sense across a range of wildcard scenarios , then it is likely to be a good idea to do anyway . <p> However , longer-term risk mitigations are often outcompeted by shorter-term objectives , more tangible outcomes and near-term priorities . National security organisations pride themselves on being agile when responding to new and emerging threats . But the key challenge is not to be responsive . Rather , organisations should aim to be resilient . Actual resilience comes through the preparation , not just the thinking . <p> The world has changed and so should our approach to analysing it . Scenario planning is just one of many forecasting tools used by security and defence professionals . We should update our approach and include more deductive techniques to complement strategic decision making . <p> Author <p> Kyle McCurdy is a technologist and former British diplomat . He has 15 years ' experience in operationalising emerging technologies , working in cyber , partnering with new companies and innovating within government .

Survey work done by Energy Consumers Australia found that about one in three homeowner households on mains gas say they will probably cancel their supply within a decade . <p> That energy has to go somewhere . And where it 's going is onto electricity distribution networks that were never designed to carry it . <p> Figure 1 shows where the problem lies . Residential heating ( the red band ) dominates Victorian gas demand in winter , reaching around 580 terajoules per day at peak . In summer it drops to near zero . <p> Heat pumps are far more efficient than the ducted gas systems they replace , delivering three to four units of heat for every unit of electricity , compared to the 60 -- 80 per cent seasonal efficiency of gas ducting . <p> But even after accounting for that gain , replacing the peak winter heating load with electricity would require the equivalent of roughly two million home batteries ( at 15 kWh each ) , fully discharged , every day @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , you 'd need to fill them all again . <p> Victoria 's electricity grid was built on the assumption that gas would carry this winter heating peak . Around two million households rely on gas for space heating , which has historically kept the electricity system summer-peaking . The mass uptake of heat pumps ( each drawing between 2 and 5 kilowatts ) is inverting that profile . <p> Because heat pump demand is driven by the weather rather than by individual habits , the load is highly coincident : hundreds of households on the same low-voltage feeder all drawing hard at the same time , on the same cold evening . The aggregate demand can exceed the thermal ratings of street-level transformers , or depress voltage at the end of long feeders below statutory limits before any thermal rating is breached . <p> And here is a point that deserves more attention : the consumer energy resources ( CER ) that usually help manage distribution stress offer limited relief for this specific problem . <p> Rooftop solar output is at its lowest precisely when heating demand peaks : @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ typically sized for daily solar cycling , are not designed to offset sustained heating loads across long winter nights . Distribution transformers will bear the full brunt of heat pump demand without much help from CER during the critical winter peak . The usual playbook does n't apply . <h> The clustering problem <p> This risk does n't arrive gradually or uniformly . The AEMC 's own CEPA modelling identifies a " switching point , " the gas tariff level at which consumers begin substituting electricity for gas . <p> For customers who remain on gas only for cooking , it 's already cheaper to switch to LPG and disconnect from the $300 / year in fixed gas network charges even if induction cooking does n't appeal . <p> The current Middle East energy crisis is adding external pressure to this dynamic . With global LNG prices surging and the government weighing new powers to secure domestic gas supply for winter , the tariff increases that trigger the switching point may arrive sooner than any domestic modelling assumed . <p> The result is sudden , localised surges in electricity demand @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Compounding the problem , commercial and light-industrial gas users ( bakeries , laundries , small manufacturers ) are frequently embedded within residential zones , sharing the same low-voltage feeders . <p> When those businesses electrify alongside surrounding households , the concentrated commercial load stacks on top of the diffuse residential heat pump load on infrastructure already under stress . <p> Here 's the critical mismatch : upgrading distribution network capacity takes three to five years from planning to commissioning . Localised gas defection can tip much faster . If the electricity grid is n't reinforced ahead of the wave , the result is either reliability failures or , perversely , households trapped on an increasingly expensive gas network because the local grid ca n't accept them . <p> And no one is joining the dots . In Victoria , gas distribution is split across three operators while electricity distribution is split across five , with service territories that do n't align . An electricity distributor using its own historical data will entirely miss the non-linear demand surges driven by gas tariff increases set by a separate , unrelated company . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is already forming <p> The limits of an economic framework become starkest when you look at what happens physically as customers leave . <p> Under current settings , permanently disconnecting from the gas network is not cheap . Supply adequacy and managed decline are mirror images of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ new philosophy . " <p> This is a tough call from the man who once sketched Richard Nixon with a pig-like face and more than hot air coming out of his rear end , and Ronald Reagan as a vampire with a terrified Statue of Liberty in his arms . His feet are encased in comfy slippers , a slight dissonance . <p> Steadman and his late wife , Anna Deverson , bought their stately house from Richard Boyle , the 9th Earl of Shannon , in 1980 . The Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment ( Strategic Reserve ) Bill 2026 gives Export Finance Australia new powers to purchase fuel from international markets and underwrite supply arrangements to keep it flowing into Australia . <p> Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen was direct about the pressure driving the move . The initial focus is on antimony , gallium and rare earth elements , all essential inputs for clean energy technology , advanced manufacturing and defence applications . <p> Minister for Resources Madeleine @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and national security position . <p> She added that critical minerals and rare earths are " at the heart of our economic and national security and are crucial for clean energy technology , advanced manufacturing and defence applications . " <p> For businesses operating in or adjacent to the minerals and resources sector , the reserve is framed as an opportunity as much as a protection measure . The government 's stated aim is to boost onshore processing of critical minerals , which would flow through to local jobs and more stable domestic supply chains . <p> Minister for Trade Don Farrell pointed to the trade dimension , noting Australia 's existing strengths in critical minerals deposits and its reputation as a reliable supplier to international partners . <p> Farrell also flagged that the reserve is designed to strengthen supply chain partnerships with key trading allies including the United States , Japan , South Korea , Europe , Canada and the UK , moves that could open doors for Australian businesses further down those supply chains .

@@136147935 <p> As rooftop solar uptake spreads to all corners of the globe , the problem of how to manage distributed generation in cities with tropical climates -- where rolling thunderstorms regularly eclipse the sun -- is becoming increasingly acute . But what if cars could come to the rescue ? <p> New research published this week has demonstrated how electric vehicles ( EVs ) could better enable the large-scale adoption of solar PV in tropical cities by storing solar and acting as temporary grid capacity when clouds roll in . <p> In a paper published in the prestigious Nature journal , researchers from Columbia University in the United States and the Singapore-ETH Centre highlighted the potential role that electric vehicles could play in mitigating the downsides of building solar PV systems in tropical cities . <p> One of the authors of the paper , civil engineer Markus Schl ? pfer , moved to Singapore a decade ago and began noticing the emerging engineering challenge of afternoon thunderstorms , which can plunge entire neighbourhoods into temporary moments of darkness . <p> Standalone storage is obviously one solution -- as is being @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ community and home batteries -- but Schl ? pfer and his colleagues considered a second option , one that would avoid expensive infrastructure buildouts . <p> " If you have a thunderstorm moving over an area with solar energy , you can have your electric cars that are parked serve as the energy source and balance out this lack of energy generation , " said Schl ? pfer , assistant professor of civil engineering and engineering mechanics at Columbia Engineering . <p> " When the thunderstorm moves away , the cars are charged again by the photovoltaics . " <p> Tropical thunderstorms do not necessarily last for long , and can often affect some neighbourhoods and not others , despite their proximity . As such , electricity can be transported from neighbouring regions that are generating power , but even if the journey is only a mile or two , the amount of electricity flowing through powerlines can often overwhelm the grid 's capacity . <p> Tropical thunderstorms lead to additional stress on electricity grids <p> Traditionally , in order to fix the problem , new infrastructure is required that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but this can be expensive -- especially in dense cities like Singapore , where underground transmission lines , for example , cost around 60 million Singapore dollars per kilometre ( around $A66.7 million ) . <p> " Building new infrastructure is extremely challenging and expensive in dense cities , " Schl ? pfer said . <p> " This is a way to use the existing network in a more efficient way and integrate more solar photovoltaics , which would otherwise need more transmission line capacity . " <p> That 's where electric car batteries could potentially come into play , according to Schl ? pfer and his colleagues . When a thunderstorm rolls over a particular neighbourhood or region , nearby parked EVs discharge their stored energy into the local grid , absorbing the shortfall without the need for transporting electricity from elsewhere . And when the storm passes , the solar panels are able to quickly recharge the cars . <p> " Car batteries can feed in the electricity stored in their batteries to the grid , " Schl ? pfer explained . <p> " We do not need @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ we do not need to install a new cable . " <p> The research also demonstrates that EV ownership does not have to be particularly high in a particular neighbourhood for the method to work . " This solution is really working in very car-light environments , " Schl ? pfer said . " We need only a small number of cars , and it works . " <p> Joshua S. @@136147961 <h> Nuclear -- now climate change : Great powers plague the Pacific <p> Media editor Dr Lee Duffield reviews the latest edition of the definitive account of the sinking of the Rainbow Warrior <p> Updated research has shown up lingering headaches over the impacts of decades-long nuclear testing in the Pacific islands and interventions of outside powers , amid growing threats from climate change , writes Dr Lee Duffield . <p> THE JOURNALIST , Professor and peace activist David Robie , was one of a media party on the ill-fated voyage of the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior ( 1955 ) , in 1985 , before its sinking by French security operatives in Auckland Harbour . He wrote a definitive book about the lead-up in the region to the fatal sinking of the ship with explosive mines ; unmasking of the plot made in Paris ; attempts to obtain justice and a long aftermath with demands for empowerment by former " colonial " people , to prevent such outrages in their island homelands . <p> The book is Eyes of Fire , published in 1986 , then successively updated as the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ outrage coming to light . It ran to three revised editions , the last out now to commemorate 40 years since the attack took place . It therefore marked 40 years since the death of the Greenpeace photographer Fernando Pereira , a Portuguese-born Dutch national , aged 35 , father of one child , drowned on board after the second of two blasts that hit the ship . <p> Eyes of Fire is a highly professional work of journalism , built out of investigation and documentation of facts , then fashioned into an accessible read ; illustrated also with easy-to-comprehendmaps and diagrams , showing where the ship travelledand where the bombs were planted against its hull , plus photographs from a copious accumulation built up as the Greenpeace movement generated publicity for its actions worldwide . <h> VOYAGE OF THE WARRIOR <p> One section describes the Rainbow Warrior , appreciatively and affectionately : a former fisheries research vessel , a trawler type , 50-metres in length , with some difficulty converted for sail as well as power , made into a ' proud campaign ship ' , painted a strong @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ' The wheelhouse was rather lumpy and unattractive but the rest of the ship was appealing . She had a high North Sea prow , graceful sheerline and round-the-corner stern . ' <h> For the record ... <p> The Rainbow Warrior sailed from Hawaii -- taking on board seven journalists and some leading figures from the Pacific communities , to the Marshall Islands -- where it evacuated the inhabitants of a nuclear afflicted island , Rongelap , to an uninhabited island Mejatto in its archipelago . Pacific distances are great . They transported 350 people -- with lumber and belongings -- in four trips , 250-kilometres there and back . The islanders were suffering from contamination by the infamous upwind explosion of the experimental thermonuclear weapon , Castle Bravo , in 1954 -- causing thyroid disorders , cancers and constant miscarriages and birthing disorders . Dissatisfied that health officials sent by the United States administration were more interested in research than care , they decided to leave . The key instigator was Marshall Islands legislator Senator Jeton Anjain . He was one of two Pacific Islands leaders with prominent roles @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Temaru , a town mayor in Tahiti , also elected as the territory 's President on five occasions . <p> Temaru spoke for many when he said : <p> " The sad truth is that the only ones who tried to help us are the Greenpeace ecologists ... " <p> A native American woman named Eyes of Fire had told a Greenpeace member about a legend , that where there was dispossession and despoilation of the land and culture , in time mythical warriors -- deliverers -- would come , who would mend and restore both . So the peace-ship offering aid would be a Rainbow Warrior . <p> The author , Robie , in his news despatches for Radio New Zealand , judged the evacuation project a change for Greenpeace towards humanitarian work connected with environmental destruction : <p> " This is n't a game or the sort of action publicity stunt that Greenpeace would do so successfully . " <p> But the next part of the journey was another dramatic action , in Marshall Islands , at the U.S. missile testing base on Kwajalein Atoll . A party @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and hoisted a banner inscribed " Stop Star Wars " onto a space tracking dome , escaping before the arrival of security guards . The banner was a reference to the American Strategic Defence Initiative , " Star Wars " , testing for which had increased the heavy traffic of missiles of different levels at the Kwajalein range ( dubbed by the empire as the Ronald Reagan Ballistic Missile Defense Site ) . <p> The scene was then being set for the tragedy as the vessel made its way 5000-kilometres to Auckland through friendly territory , calling in at Kiribati , the former Christmas Island base for British nuclear tests ( 1957-58 ) , and Vanuatu , where the leader of the then five year-old Republic , Father Walter Lini , a champion for a nuclear free Pacific , organised a big public welcome . <h> THE STRIKE <p> Celebration fitted the mood of the " Warrior " crew a lot of the time , in this account ; a group of eleven skilled and idealistic younger people , sharing a mission they considered important to the world , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ nature and promote peace , never violent , but charismatic , given to direct action , often enough dangerous . They had 14 others on board -- in the case of David Robie , for an extended time , 11 days , time enough to get to know the characters and introduce them to readers in his book . <p> A further leg of the voyage was intended , to take them to Mururoa Atoll -- where France was continuing with underground nuclear testing -- as flagship for a flotilla of protest boats . In the event , the flotilla sailed , led by another Greepenace ship , Greenpeace III . One boat was arrested penetrating the 12-kilometre territorial limit around the Atoll , where a series of tests was about to begin . <p> The planned disruption of activities on Mururoa may have been the death warrant for Rainbow Warrior -- a solution to the riddle of what purposes its destruction was supposed to serve.As the ship made its way towards Auckland , two French infiltrators got to work in that City , penetrating the Greenpeace operation . A @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ was en route to New Zealand on a charter boat and two officers of France 's security service , DGSE , Dominique Prieur and Alain Mafart , flew in under cover as a honeymoon couple . <p> Rainbow Warrior came in on Sunday 7 July 1985 , surrounded by an escort of small boats and was sunk at the dock in shallow water just before midnight on 10 July . Divers using an inflatable boat set off the two explosions . Prieur and Mafart were spotted picking up one of the divers on a beach by men doing night watch at their boat club , who got the number of their vehicle , enabling the police to apprehend them , and begin a tortured process to try and secure justice . <p> Rainbow Warrior , Woodside protest ( Image supplied ) <h> AFTERMATH <p> Updating of the book takes in the negotiations over holding Prieur and Mafart , their eventual transfer to France and subsequent early release ; the fate of other conspirators spiritedhome , promoted , decorated , " looked after " in early retirement ; intensive and large @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about the charter boat carrying some of the divers , said to have transferred them onto a submarine , the Rubis ; investigative work by the French press to sheet home responsibility for the attack . <p> Very soon after Rainbow Warrior was sunk , the Defence Minister , Charles Hernu , was sacked and the head of the DGSE Admiral Pierre Lacoste resigned . In office for four years in 1985 , it may have been a new Government still failing to face down entrenched security identities , undisciplined , considering themselves to be " deep state " , attached to violent solutions , with potential to go rogue . <p> Most of Robie 's work here is a narrative , a strong true story , but it has space for analysis , and in particular registers the correlation between devastation brought by the nuclear testing , and colonial management and manipulation of islands affairs . The post-War wave of independence had come to the Pacific , though not to French Polynesia nor New Caledonia . In addition @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ trust or , for Sovereign states , via signed compacts of free association , accompanied by substantial aid payments . ' <p> David Robie reports on the 40th anniversary commemoration of the 1985 events by Greenpeace , sending the new purpose-built ship , the new Rainbow Warrior ( 2011 ) , sometimes known as Rainbow Warrior III , to carry out independent radiation research . " <h> Note on the reviewer ... <p> Dr Lee Duffield reported on Australia 's dispute with France over atmospheric testing for ABC News in Sydney and then from Paris as the ABC European Correspondent . @@136176728 <h> While the Coalition claims electric trucks are not capable of transporting heavy freight , overseas usage and current trials in Australia show they far outperform diesel on both overall cost and efficiency . By Mike Seccombe . <h> B-doubling down on electric trucks <p> New Energy Transport 's Windrose truck is loaded in Sydney before embarking on Australia 's first end-to-end all-electric freight delivery between Sydney and Canberra last month . <p> Bridget McKenzie , the National Party 's leader in the Senate , was contemptuous . <p> During an urgency motion on March 30 about the government 's response to the global fuel crisis , she fired up over suggestions that Australia should look at electrifying the country 's heavy vehicle fleet . <p> " To hear the ridiculous contributions from the Labor Party senators , who somehow think you can hook up a B-double full of cattle , coming down from Rockhampton to Brisbane , and actually use an electric truck ? Seriously ? " <p> McKenzie , who is also the Coalition 's spokesperson for transport , continued : " I 'm all for electric where @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ capital cities , where you can plug it in at night . " <p> It is , however , indeed possible to move cattle , or steel , toilet paper and many other things , on a giant semi with an electric prime mover at the front , and to do it more cheaply and quickly than with diesel . It 's already happening in much of the rest of the world -- and now , somewhat belatedly , in this country . <p> The EV revolution is moving on from light to heavy vehicles , and doing so at an astonishing pace . <p> The 2025 Global EV Outlook report from the International Energy Agency recorded an 80 per cent increase in electric truck sales globally in 2024 . There 's been an almost six-fold increase in the number of available models , to more than 400 , since 2020 . <p> More recent data , published by CV World , a Chinese website specialising in the commercial vehicle market , is even more startling . Total registrations of what it called " new energy vehicles " -- mostly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- was up 182 per cent year on year in China in 2025 . <p> More than 45,000 heavy-duty electric trucks were registered -- 54 per cent of total registrations -- in just the month of December . <p> Advances in batteries and charging infrastructure are catalysts . New heavy-duty electric trucks can travel 400-500 kilometres on a single charge , making them suitable for many regional freight routes and long-distance corridors . <p> A new generation of megawatt charging infrastructure makes it possible for an electric semi to charge from 20 per cent to 80 per cent in less than 30 minutes . <p> Had McKenzie even paid attention to what was happening outside the Parliament House door that Monday , she might have avoided embarrassment . <p> The Smart Energy Council had arranged , on the lawns at the front of the house , a display of several heavy electric trucks . They were there at 7am , ahead of a gathering of some 300 industry , government , energy and infrastructure representatives in Parliament 's Great Hall for the Freight Forward 2026 summit on commercial vehicle decarbonisation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ organisers say the event on the front lawn was open to anyone to attend . Had she fronted up , she might have learnt a lot . <p> One of those trucks displayed on the parliament lawns was a Chinese-made , B-double rated , Windrose prime mover . Over about the past six months , Windrose and Australian company New Energy Transport have engaged in a series of trials and demonstrations of the capabilities of electrics . <p> Last October the truck completed a 480-kilometre round trip from Picton , south of Sydney , to Beresfield in the Hunter region on a single charge , with a load of feed provided by Australia 's largest poultry transport , logistics and engineering services provider , Multiquip . <p> The person charged by Multiquip with ensuring the truck met all relevant laws and regulations -- which it did -- was the company 's national compliance manager , David Muir . <p> Muir came to the trial , he says , with no prior experience of the type of truck , nor preconceptions about the relative merits of electric versus diesel . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The Windrose produces 1400 horsepower -- compared with 500 to 700 from a typical diesel -- which enables it to maintain speed , even up steep gradients . <p> Muir says he wo n't repeat exactly what other truck drivers said over the two-way " when it was flying past them , up Mount White " . The gist of it was , they were impressed . <p> " Electric trucking is the opposite . It 's high capex , low opex . The trucks are more expensive up front , and you have to pay for charging infrastructure , but the benefits on the other side , on the opex side , are so huge that the overall cost , we believe , is now lower than diesel . " <p> Because the Windrose was able to sit at the speed limit the whole way , the trip was also 40 minutes faster than it would have been under diesel power . <p> Moreover , the fuel cost was a fraction of the diesel alternative , says Daniel Bleakley , co-founder and co-chief executive of New Energy Transport . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cents wholesale renewable energy price , that would have cost about $50 up and back for a 36-tonne combination . <p> " That trip normally costs around $300 in diesel , at prewar prices , " he says . <p> Bleakley says a recent delivery from Sydney to Canberra with a load of toilet paper from Who Gives a Crap cost about 84 per cent less than the equivalent diesel run , based on current prices . <p> " Even on pre-Iran war , pre-oil crisis prices , we estimate that that run would have still been 70 per cent cheaper on energy cost alone . @@136176744 <h> Ed Husic Beyond the data centre hype <p> I have a confession to make : growing up in Western Sydney , I really did n't like summer . It may seem an odd declaration , when celebrating sun , blue sky and surf is such a dominant feature of Australia 's national psyche . <p> No one mentions sweltering in woefully designed homes unable to withstand blistering January days or the nights that follow . They were n't houses ; they were brick-veneer hotboxes . There was also something about the topography of Western Sydney that captured the heat , which fed off wide , treeless stretches of bitumen and concrete . <p> Rising record temperatures , fuelled by global warming and climate change , have made these heat traps even harder to avoid . <p> So is it any wonder local councils in Western Sydney will cast a sceptical gaze over any development that adds to -- rather than alleviates -- heat in the region ? Increasingly , their attention is drawn to the raft of development applications for data centres . <p> Roughly three quarters of New @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ concentrated in Western Sydney . A decent chunk is located where I grew up : the Blacktown local government area . The corridor stretching from Eastern Creek through to Marsden Park has become a cluster of data centre developments . Penrith City Council is now raising concerns too . <p> Why ? Data centre operators prefer their sites in cooler climates , where it is easier to manage the heat emitted by rack after rack of computing power and data storage . The space -- not to mention the necessary power and water supply -- to accommodate that is a scarcity , however . For data centre developers , that means : build where you can . <p> The Western Sydney Regional Organisation of Councils is especially concerned about the cumulative and poorly understood impacts of heat generation , noise and emissions caused by the concentration of data centres , given that the applications are assessed on their individual merits , rather than collectively . But this is n't only a Western Sydney issue ; it has become a national one . Australia is grappling with a data centre frenzy . <p> Growing opposition to data centre developments among regional communities in the United States means American tech companies are increasingly desperate to find other locations for the rollout of energy-guzzling data centres . <p> What has agitated US communities is not just the large physical footprint of data centres . It 's their resource demands and the question of who truly foots the bill . Typical data centres -- of about five to 10 megawatts in capacity -- can use roughly the same amount of power as 10,000 houses . They are among the fastest-growing sources of electricity demand in Australia , with a similar appetite to aluminium smelters . They require nonstop electricity supply , placing pressure on generation , transmission and distribution systems in a way traditional commercial loads never have . According to the Climate Council , a one-gigawatt data centre planned for Sydney will be " one of the biggest data centres in the world , using the equivalent of almost half the power from Victoria 's Loy Yang A coal power plant " . <p> An energy grid in fundamental transition -- as ours is -- will not be prepared to handle this premature , extreme level of demand . Nor is the US grid . Bloomberg analysis has shown that wholesale electricity costs in American communities located near data centres have increased by 267 per cent in just five years , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ There is also the issue of emissions . A United Nations agency warned that emissions from the highest-emitting AI systems could soon produce 102.6 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent a year . As Australia works fervently to lift our supply of renewable energy , data centres have begun to rely on coal-generated energy , which has seen their emissions double in five years , according to the Clean Energy Regulator . <p> Advocates for data centre construction in Australia even brazenly argued recently for nuclear power options to support data centre energy demand . That 's despite last year 's federal election having proved beyond doubt that nuclear power was as attractive an idea as Peter Dutton becoming prime minister . <p> There 's a lot that makes Australia attractive to US tech giants . We are a Five Eyes security partner , committed to a renewable energy rollout , with plenty of land and multiple states vying to be the " data centre capital " . Moreover , Australia nowadays is all about embracing the upsides of AI , without focusing too much on the messy downsides . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ serve them , these companies are ramping up pressure , declaring regulation " the enemy of growth " and friction that slows future gains , and warning that Australia ca n't be left behind in the global AI race . Their economic scale translates into political influence , technical dominance and a negotiating power that can exceed that of national governments . <p> This creates a paradox . As I stared at this figure , Portrait of a young man , his gaze followed me and left me with questions about who he was and where exactly he was from . <p> As a historian , I am aware of the presence of people of African descent in the distant past , but knowing something and seeing tangible evidence of that existence are two very different things . I have never encountered objects this old that speak to histories of Black people in ancient Rome . <p> I was being led through ROME : Empire , Power , People , an exhibition at Melbourne Museum that features more than 150 objects from two institutions in Italy . " <p> Supratik Baralay , an assistant professor of classics at Princeton University , agrees that the figure appears dignified , owing to both the fine craftsmanship and the use of this specific type of marble -- a material that was not only expensive but also difficult to carve , and therefore not commonly seen . Baralay is particularly struck by how isolated the portrait feels . " This is a way for a museum to show how exceptional the portrait is , but it is also perhaps a tacit recognition of how enigmatic it remains , " he says .
